He gets to the platform for work and gets on the other train instead, and cannot say why. Some pull he doesn't examine puts him on the coast line, and by the time he understands what he's doing he's already walking out onto frozen sand, and there's a woman with dyed hair standing on it like she's been waiting, though neither of them could say for what.

Inside his own head, hours earlier, the last room had still been standing: the shore house, the night they met, glass still unbroken in the frame. Ivy in the doorway telling him to walk out, and then, quieter, to come and find her at the coast. He hadn't understood it as an instruction. He understands it now, watching her cross the sand toward him.

The machine had finished sometime before dawn. He woke with a headache and a flatness he couldn't name, and there was nobody in his head who hadn't been there two years before. Before that, deeper in the night, Dell and the receptionist had been dancing on his bed in their underwear, drinking his beer, while the map on the screen quietly stopped meaning anything and nobody noticed for a long time. Before that, Tobias had been running through his own memories, dragging her into rooms she'd never stood in — a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map didn't reach — because somewhere in the deleting he had changed his mind and there was no one to tell.

He drives her back into the city, and she talks to him too easily for a stranger, and he lets himself believe that's just how some people are.

Before the running, there had been the watching: room after room losing its walls while he stood inside them, the worst of it going first, the shouting, the silences, the door. Before that, the technicians letting themselves into his flat at night, one of them slipping the bagged keepsakes — hairslide, mug, torn page — into his own coat while the other worked the machine. Before that, Tobias handing over two carrier bags of everything that had her in it, so a man he'd never met could find the exact spot to cut.

Outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time, and he goes, and it is easy, wrongly easy, in a way he doesn't ask questions about yet.

Before the bags, there had been the office, the form letter Nina and Grady had put in his hand, the director's calm face telling him yes, it could be done, that afternoon if he liked. Before that, the bookshop, and Ivy looking at him the way you look at a customer, laughing at everything the young man behind the counter said. Before that, a shabby clinic where she had paid to have a man taken out of her head, every room, every argument, every good afternoon, as though he had never been in it.

They sit in a stairwell, later, two envelopes open between them, and listen to their own recorded voices give the clinic all the reasons why. Her voice describing the drinking. His voice describing what he'd learned to withhold. She runs down two flights and he thinks that's the end of it, and then she comes back up.

Before the tapes, there had been a receptionist emptying filing cabinets on her way out the door, mailing every patient their own file, their own voice, their own reasons. Before that, a hallway at three in the morning, a kiss, a wife arriving to explain to Rosa exactly why she had always felt that way about the director and could no longer remember. Before all of it — two years of it, the ice on the river, steam on a noodle-house window, the drive-in with the sound down — there had been a cold beach at the end of the rail line, a man with nothing to say to anyone, a woman with dyed hair, a shuttered house, a broken window, two people asleep on the boards with the whole ruin of it still ahead of them.

"Anyway," she says, on the stairs, wiping her face. "I'm not going anywhere."

He doesn't know what that costs her to say. He says it anyway too.

There is a room where a heart is put into a chest that has been failing for weeks, and the man wakes up in the dark listening to it as if it belonged to someone else, which it does. There is a room, elsewhere, or maybe the same night, where a woman is told twice in a row that her family is gone, first the husband, then, before she has finished with that, both girls. There is a pickup that comes through a crossing and does not stop, then stops, then goes again. There is a man behind a motel with a gun against his own ribs, refusing to use it on the person he came to kill, telling him instead to run.

None of this happens in the order you would want it to.

Aaron Vale is a mathematician who cannot make the stairs anymore, and a doctor draws him a picture of his own heart failing on a piece of paper, and his wife Della, who has been gone from the house a year, comes back with a form from a clinic and asks him to sign while there is still a version of him that can. He signs nothing. He is thinking about weeks, not children.

Lena Ward gardens, drives her girls to school, has been clean long enough to stop counting the days. Her husband adores her in the unhurried way of someone who has never had reason not to.

Wes Tarrow preaches to boys on Saturdays with scripture inked into his forearms, testifies to strangers, and his wife Nita watches him the way you watch a sky that might turn.

The pickup hits the crossing. It stops, sits with the engine running, backs up a little, and then goes on. Somewhere a chest is opened; a heart that was beating an hour earlier in somebody else is put into it. Aaron wakes able to breathe. Lena is told, twice, in the same room.

Wes walks into a police station on his own two feet and tells the desk sergeant everything, the crossing, the distance he drove after. He is back inside within the month. Lena starts using again in the bathroom of a bar, then in her own kitchen with the girls' drawings still taped to the wall behind her, because there is nothing left to protect them from.

Aaron cannot stop wondering whose it was. He pays a man in a car park who tells him this is against every rule there is and then hands him a name and a street anyway. He learns which pool she swims at and arranges to be in the water until it isn't a coincidence anymore. Within a fortnight he is in her house. He tells Della he isn't coming back, that he doesn't want the child from the freezer after all, and she tells him the true thing — that he is spending a life somebody else paid for.

He tells Lena in her own kitchen, badly, what is beating in his chest. She throws him out that night. Four days later she asks him back, knowing exactly what she's taking in.

Released early, Wes gets as far as the prison gate, sees his family waiting, and keeps walking. He takes a job cleaning rooms at a motel four hundred miles from anyone who knows his name, and puts down his faith somewhere along that road the same way he put down Nita.

Lena says she cannot breathe in the same country as the man who did it, says it until it's the only sentence in the house. Aaron buys a gun from someone in a lock-up and drives to the motel with it under the seat. He gets Wes against a wall in the dark and cannot make his hand finish it. The shot lands somewhere survivable. He tells him to get up and run.

Wes follows them back to their own room instead, bleeding through his shirt, and asks to be finished. Aaron turns the gun around and puts it into himself.

They get him into a car, drive with the horn down the whole way, and the borrowed heart stops on the table regardless of the speed. Wes goes back to the family he walked out on. Lena goes home alone, carrying something that hasn't happened yet and now, somehow, already has.

The warehouse smelled like diesel and old rope, and Mr. Ash was holding him the way you hold something you're afraid will slip through your fingers if you loosen up even a little. "Nobody dies here today," he kept saying, like saying it enough times made it a law of physics. Danny's shirt was soaked black through and he couldn't tell anymore where the blood ended and the man's hands began.

It had gone wrong inside a minute. The alarm was already screaming when they came out the side door, and Ash had fired through the windshield and both side windows while Cal drove them the wrong way down a one-way street. On foot after that, no car, no plan, Danny had pulled a woman out of her own Honda and she'd had a pistol in the door pocket and used it before he got the door shut. He'd shot her. He didn't remember deciding to. He remembered driving after, one hand on the wheel and one pressed into his own stomach like he could hold himself in that way.

He thought, lying on the concrete now with Ash's hand under his skull, of the room Pruitt had put him in six months back, no furniture, just two chairs and a story about a bag of drugs and four dogs in a public toilet. Pruitt had made him tell it forty times until it stopped sounding like a story and started sounding like something that had actually happened to him, until the details arrived without him reaching for them. He'd told it to Bram and Cal and Mr. Ash in a bar with the practiced ease of a man showing off an old scar, and they'd laughed in the right place, and that was that. Mr. Elm. A name off a list, colour-free, chosen for him.

The list itself had come out of Bram's mouth over a diner argument about whether a pop song was really about heartbreak or about something dirtier, and whether the waitress deserved an extra dollar for refilling coffee nobody asked her to refill. Ren had been there too, fresh out, having done years he could've shaved off by talking and hadn't, and Bram had put an envelope and a place on the job in front of him like a man settling a bar tab. Then the tree names, Bram dealing them out so no one in the room could name anyone else if it came to that, and Mr. Birch spending a full minute complaining that his was the ugliest one on the list.

Now Birch was here too, clean, furious, saying the police had been on the pavement before the first alarm even went, which meant somebody in this room had made a call. He'd gone out after that and put the diamonds somewhere none of them would find without him.

And then Ren came in late, unbothered, complaining about the noise, and opened his trunk and dragged out a bound patrolman named Doyle.

Left alone with him, Ren had found an oldies station on a little radio, turned it up, danced a few steps like he had all the time in the world, and taken the man's ear off with a razor before soaking him in gasoline.

Danny had shot him from the floor. Everything he had left went into it. Then, because the man on the chair had earned something for what he'd just watched, Danny told him: I'm a cop, there are cars outside waiting on Bram.

Cal came back to a corpse and a story and decided the story would do — then put three rounds into Doyle himself to make sure nobody else would ever ask him to confirm it.

Bram walked in last, looked at Danny on the floor, and said, flatly, that's the one. Ash turned his gun on his own boss rather than believe it.

Three guns went off at once in that small room. When it stopped, only Ash and Danny were still breathing.

"Say it," Ash told him, and Danny did, plainly, because the man deserved that much. Ash put the barrel to his own head as the doors came down, and the officers took him before the trigger finished its work, and Danny went still on the concrete a moment after, the lie finally, completely, over.

In the unfinished palace they call Silvermount, Emmett Rusk died with a single word on his lips and let a small glass globe roll from his fingers. It rolled off the boards and broke on the step, and the nurse down the corridor did not come in time to hear what he'd said.

The newsreel that ran in every theater that week gave nine minutes to his life — the boy who inherited a fortune from a mining claim, the newspaper he bought and remade, the two marriages, the governor's race he lost, the palace on the hill — and explained nothing at all. A reporter named Nash was sent to find out what "Bluebell" meant, since that was the word the nurse thought she'd caught, and he began with the widow, the second one, Nora, who was drunk at a table in a seaside club at four in the afternoon and told him to get out before he'd finished his sentence.

So he went looking elsewhere, and the looking took him backward through the whole of it.

He read Barrow's memoir first, in a marble library that still smelled of packing straw, and there was the beginning of the story: a boarding house out west, a lodger who couldn't pay his rent and left a mine deed instead, and a mother who signed her son over to the banker the day the seam proved enormous, while the boy's father objected uselessly from the doorway. There was the boy on a sled, driving it into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down, and being taken east anyway that same evening.

Marsh remembered the morning it all became Emmett's, the fortune and the list of holdings, and the young man asking for the one thing on it that lost money — a newspaper called the Clarion — because he thought running it might be fun. Marsh remembered the bed moved into the office, the statement of principles set in type over Emmett's own signature, the whole rival staff hired away and a party thrown for them with a brass band and a chorus line, Emmett dancing in the middle of it.

Devlin, found finally in another city, in a smaller newsroom, talked about the marriage to Adele, the governor's niece, brought home from a buying trip like a piece of statuary — and about the breakfasts after, growing longer and colder, until husband and wife sat at opposite ends of the table reading rival papers, one of which Emmett owned. He talked about the shopgirl Nora Kell, met by accident in the mud outside a chemist's, and the secret visits, and the ten days before the election when the party boss Halloran brought Adele up the stairs to Nora's rooms and offered a trade Emmett refused to take. He talked about the six-column headline crying fraud, about asking for a transfer, about a promise that was worth nothing.

Nora, sober the second time Nash came, talked the longest. About being married and then bought a teacher, then a house to sing in, because Emmett had decided the world would think of her as a singer whether or not she was one. About the debut, and Devlin drunk over half a written sentence, and Emmett finishing it in the same cruel direction and printing it and firing him. About the poison, and being allowed, finally, to stop. About Silvermount, and the jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station, and the black-sand picnic, and packing her bags while he told her, in the only language he had, that she could not go.

The butler Colm was the one who remembered the bedroom torn apart afterward, and the glass globe found among the wreckage, and the one word said to no one before it was carried past a pair of facing mirrors.

Nash closed his notebook in the marble library and decided that no single word ever explains a life. Below him, workmen were clearing the last of the unopened crates from the great hall, and among the junk was a small sled, its paint gone gray, one word still faintly visible along the runner. They put it into the furnace with everything else, and it burned, and nobody left in the house that afternoon had ever heard the name Bluebell at all.

THE BRIEFCASE

Rollo drove and Marcus argued with him about what a hamburger was called in countries neither of them had visited, and about drug laws in places they would never see, because the job was still forty minutes off and neither man wanted to name it yet. By the time they stood in the corridor outside the flat, guns still zipped in a gym bag, they had moved on to whether rubbing another man's wife's feet was worth being thrown off a balcony for. Marcus thought it depended on the balcony. Then the door was in front of them and there was nothing left to argue.

Marcus said a line of scripture to the boy on the other side of it before they shot him. Tobin had skimmed from Otis and this was the arithmetic of that. They took the briefcase off the table. A fourth man they hadn't accounted for came out of the bathroom and fired a revolver six times from six feet and missed with all six, and Marcus stood in front of the ruined wall behind him and said that was God, plainly, the way another man might say it was raining.

In the car Rollo's gun went off over nothing and took Del's head off the back seat, and Marcus drove the wreck to Warren's, where a soft, unhurried man hosed them down in the yard and put them into borrowed shorts and T-shirts and had the car gone before lunch.

They still had the briefcase. They carried it into Otis's bar dressed like students, and Otis was at the counter paying a boxer named Denny to go down in the fifth, and did not ask why his men were dressed for the beach. He only took the case.

Before any of that, over eggs at a counter that morning, two strangers had decided nobody ever robbed a restaurant, and were up on the booth seats with a pistol out before the plates were cleared, and it was Marcus — the same morning, the miracle still on him — who let himself be robbed, handed over his own wallet, said his line of scripture again, and explained that he had decided what it meant. He kept the case. He let them walk.

THE WATCH

Years before, a man home from years of captivity sat a boy down and put a gold watch into his hands, the one his father had kept hidden the whole time, and told him what it had cost to keep. Denny wore it after that the way some men wear a name.

He wore it into the ring the night Otis paid him to lose in the fifth, and he did not lose; he hit the other man hard enough that the man never got up, and was in a taxi before the crowd understood what they'd seen.

In the motel he asked Marielle if she'd packed it. She hadn't. It was on the table in the flat, in the one place he couldn't go.

He went anyway. He found the watch exactly where it had been left, and a man came out of the bathroom with a gun he hadn't drawn fast enough, because the submachine gun on the counter was nearer to Denny than his own was to him. Rollo went down in the doorway. Denny put the watch on his wrist and left with the heroin's near-victim still unknown to him — the same bag that, days earlier, had put Nadia blue on a carpet after Rollo bought it pure from Kip and danced her round a themed diner they'd won a contest at, and revived her with a needle to the chest on a stranger's floor.

Martin sits on the edge of a bed he does not remember taking, the phone cord looped around two fingers, telling a stranger about a man named Elias Prine who lost his memory and killed his wife with insulin she asked for again and again. "I denied the claim," he says. "I thought it was in his head." The voice on the other end listens like it already knows how the story ends, and asks him to keep going.

A year earlier, out past the edge of town, Roy walks Martin through a derelict building with a flashlight and a service revolver, finds a man crouched behind a stack of pallets, and stands back while Martin puts two rounds into him. Within minutes Martin turns to Roy and asks who they were looking for. Roy says it's finished. Martin believes him, because Martin believes whatever he's told last.

The voice on the phone gives Martin a name — Gil, a dealer, an address, a time. Martin copies it onto the pad by the lamp as though writing scripture.

Before that, in a house with the windows boarded, Martin fills a coffee can with matches and burns his wife's hairbrush and a paperback with her name inside the cover, in a field where no one will see him not finish grieving.

In the basement, water standing an inch deep on the concrete, Martin beats a small man half his weight and finishes him with a belt round the throat, then takes the picture the way he takes all his pictures, for later.

Further back, before any of this, in a bright office with a water cooler humming, Martin runs Elias Prine through the same three questions four times and writes psychosomatic in blue ink, and the man across the desk says nothing, because he has already forgotten he asked.

Gil, dying, whispers a name — Elias — that means nothing to Martin, who writes it off as noise and puts on the dead man's suit, takes the dead man's keys, and drives the dead man's car into the night.

Three nights after his wife tests him with a syringe for the eleventh time and does not wake, two men come through Martin's bathroom door. He kills one across his wife's body; the other puts his head through the mirror, and after that nothing new will ever stay.

Roy finds Martin still in Gil's suit and tells him plainly: Gil was nobody, the real man died a year ago in that same derelict building, and the case Martin tells strangers down telephone lines is not a case — it is his own house, his own wife, his own hands. Martin listens the way he listens to everything, entirely, and then burns the photographs of Gil, writes HE IS LYING TO YOU across Roy's picture, and copies Roy's plate number onto a fresh page as the truest thing he owns.

Martin turns himself into a system after the mirror: instant photographs, block capitals, five facts already inked into his thigh where no fire and no forgetting can reach them.

At a parlour with a buzzing needle, Martin has Roy's plate cut into his skin as the sixth fact, not remembering that he wrote the note demanding it.

Behind her own bar, Corinne watches a stranger walk in wearing Gil's suit, driving Gil's car, and has the staff spit in his beer before they set it down.

She hides every pen in the house, says the words that make him swing, waits outside until her own face bruises, and comes back blaming a man called Vance so Martin will go finish someone who never touched her.

Elias's wife, testing whether her husband's blankness is real, asks for her injection once more, and once more, and once more, and he gives it to her every time as though for the first.

Martin waits in a motel bathroom in the dark, takes Vance down as he comes through the door, and drives him to the edge of town at gunpoint with a warning neither of them will remember him giving.

Corinne runs the plate through a friend at the registry and lays the printout on the table: Roy Mercer, in full, with an address.

And Elias Prine sits in Martin's office a second time, memory gone, claim denied again in Martin's own blue ink, though Martin will never know he has already lived this exact room from the other chair.

Martin brings Roy out to the same derelict building on a pretext, walks him into the room where a year ago a stranger died for him, and shoots him once, satisfied, at last, that the note in his pocket was right.

All night the helicopters went over, low, spraying for the fruit fly, and every house in the city heard the same noise at the same hour and thought it was about something else.

At the Hartigans', Neil changed his shirt twice and Bess worked in her studio until the last minute, among unfinished bodies, getting ready for people neither of them much wanted to see. Across town Otto the baker took an order from a woman named Elaine: a cake, a name, an age, ready Monday, please collect it promptly. In a booth with a headset and a basket of nappies, Cheryl talked a stranger through his fantasy while her husband Stu sat three feet away going quiet in the particular way that meant something. In a club with low light, Vida sang standards to people who were mostly talking, and at home her daughter Bee practiced cello into an empty house. Officer Rowe drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and put it out of the car, because he needed a reason for where he'd been, and told Peg it must have gone over the fence.

Elaine's boy Charlie stepped off the kerb on his way to school and a waitress called Rhona, in a hurry, caught him with the wing. He got up, said he was fine, wouldn't take a lift, and walked home. That night he went to sleep on the sofa and didn't wake up properly. After that there was a room with a machine in it, and Grant and Elaine taking shifts in a chair. Grant's father Duff, unseen in years, turned up with a coffee and, having nothing else to offer the silence, told his son about a woman from decades back. Nobody had come for the cake or paid for it, and Otto, bad at being ignored, started ringing the house at two in the morning to say the boy's name.

Stu and three friends, Vern among them, walked in to the good water and found a young woman face down in the shallows. They tied a line to her ankle so she wouldn't drift and fished for two more days before telling anyone. Vern's wife Iris, taking off her clown makeup at the kitchen table, heard the story the way it got told at the pub and stopped with the sponge still in her hand.

Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had someone new and spent an afternoon sawing her furniture into pieces. House-sitting the Hartigans' good address, Ike and Dot made each other up as a beaten corpse and photographed it in the hall, laughing.

At the dinner party, over the fish, Bess told Neil about the modelling session and then the thing after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene in front of everyone.

The machine was switched off in the morning. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at a man about a telephone, and Otto sat them down, put warm bread in front of them, and grieved with them, learning only then whose birthday the cake had been for.

Bee came home from rehearsal, found her mother asleep in the chair as always, walked to the garage, pulled the door down, and started the car.

At a picnic in the hills, a girl said some ordinary wrong thing, and Stu, who had been holding something in since the river, picked up a rock and brought it down on her.

The ground moved for eleven seconds that evening. By the late bulletin it had taken everything with it — the boy, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills, the wrecked furniture, the abandoned dog, the dinner party — folded into the same three minutes of news, weather among weather, as if none of it had needed anyone to cause it at all.

Above the noise, at an open window, an old man was telling a younger one that nothing anybody does survives. "Not the buildings, not the marriages, not the grudges," he said. "Time takes it all back eventually. I don't say it to be cruel. It's just the arithmetic of the thing." Below them the street was full of blue light.

The blue light was for the two men being carried out through a crowd with their hands cuffed behind them, one shouting, one gone silent, both spattered with something that wasn't paint. They were put into separate cars without being allowed to look at each other.

Before that, inside, a man had taken the fire extinguisher off the wall and gone on swinging it long after the other man had stopped moving. A few feet away, watching along with everyone else, stood the man they had actually come for, hands in his pockets, unremarked.

Before that, a stranger's arm had been taken at the elbow and turned until it came apart, because the man holding faces up out of the dark had picked the wrong one.

Before that, two men had detached themselves from a doorway outside a hospital and offered, for money, to say who had done it and where he drank. They pointed down the street toward a basement door with no sign on it.

Before that, two men had come out of a party laughing and stopped laughing at the sight of a trolley and a blanket and a face they knew.

Before that, in a tiled underpass lit orange and humming, a man had gone on hitting a woman's head against the concrete after the rest of it was already over, unhurried, while at the far end another man had looked, hesitated, and left.

Before that, the same man had had a transsexual woman by the hair, explaining something to her with his fist, when a stranger came down the stairs instead of crossing four lanes of headlights, and stopped, and was seen.

Before that, at a party, a man had been drinking past the point of being any fun, and had started working the room for someone else, and a woman had watched him do it for a while, said nothing, collected her coat, and gone.

Before that, three of them had stood swaying together in an underground carriage, arguing cheerfully about sex and about how much he'd already had to drink, the kind of argument people have when they expect to have it again tomorrow.

Before that, she had lain in a park with the sprinklers turning over the cut grass and children running through the spray, a book open and unread on the blanket, one hand resting flat on her stomach as if she were listening to something.

Before that, alone in the flat, she had sat on the edge of the bath with a white stick in both hands and let herself smile at it before telling anyone at all.

And before that, in bed, morning light coming thin through the curtains, she had told him about a dream she kept having — a tunnel, red-walled, that she walked into and could not seem to walk back out of — and the two of them had traded lazy insults about the man she used to live with, who was only a friend now, and laughed, easy with each other in the particular way of people who think they have all the time they need.

"So what did survive," the younger man asked, at the window, "if nothing does?"

The old man looked down at the street, at the blue light sliding off wet stone, at the doorway where two strangers had stood earlier that same night doing business in a dead woman's name.

"Nothing," he said. "That's rather the point. Ask them tomorrow what they were arguing about on the train, on the way there. They won't remember. They'll remember the extinguisher. They'll remember the blanket. The rest goes first, always, the ordinary part — the part that was actually theirs."

He drew the curtain halfway across, not to hide the light so much as to soften it, and said nothing further, as though the sentence itself had already gone the way of everything else he was describing.

# The Dog

The house had been built for two people and now held four adults, a baby, and a dog. Ruben slept on the couch and watched his brother's wife move through the kitchen, and his mother kept the peace by pretending not to see anything. Nestor came home some nights with a scarf still folded in his pocket and money he wouldn't explain, and when Alma asked where it came from he knocked her across the room. Ruben started saying she should come away with him. Quietly, then not.

The dog, Tigre, had come back from the street once having killed something twice its size. A neighbor told Ruben what that was worth, and within a month the animal was going into a pit twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben was hiding money in the wardrobe, thinking of it as a door.

He paid two men to hurt his brother, thinking that would clear a path. Nestor worked out who'd sent them within a day, and left with his wife, his son, and every note Ruben had saved. The dog kept fighting. A promoter named Chaco, having lost too much on one match, put a pistol into Tigre's side in the middle of the ring, and Ruben went over the rope with a knife before he'd decided to. He and his friend Pipo were in a truck and gone before anyone stood up.

He ran a red light doing sixty, dog bleeding in the back seat, and took the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

Later, much later, a vagrant named Cardo would say he had seen the whole thing from the curb — smoke, two wrecked cars, people converging — and had simply lifted the dog out of the wreck and walked off with it, the only thing anyone took from that junction that wasn't already broken.

Cardo fed the dog by hand for weeks in a yard full of strays until it slept against him and followed him into the street like something tamed. He'd once been a guerrilla; now he took contracts for men in good suits who didn't ask him what he'd been. A man named Elian met him behind a church and paid him to kill his own half-brother, Sergio, and named a price without explaining the grudge. Cardo took Sergio off a pavement without trouble, then chained him to a bed frame in his own yard instead of finishing the job, for reasons he didn't say even to himself. Later he brought Elian face to face with the brother he'd paid to erase, set a loaded pistol on the floor exactly between them, and walked out having taken money from both, done deciding for other men what should be decided.

He had watched his own wife buried among people who thought he'd died twenty years before, then followed his grown daughter Perla three streets home and stood outside her door without going in. He came home once to a yard of dead strays and Tigre standing among them with its mouth wet, and put the gun to its skull and held it there and could not fire — the one thing he'd nursed, after all the killing he'd been paid for.

He let himself into Perla's flat while she was at work, sat an hour on her bed, and left a message on her machine confessing everything — who he was, where he'd gone, why — and took one photograph off her shelf on the way out.

Across the city, a model named Celine had been moved into a flat with a window facing her own billboard by a man who'd left his wife for her. After the crash her leg was pinned with steel, and her lapdog Chispa, lost in the new rooms, fell through a gap in the floorboards and could not climb back. He tore up the boards hunting the whine while her leg went black above him. It was amputated in the end, the same week the billboard came down and left a blank frame across the street.

Nestor died on a bank floor with the same scarf in his pocket. At the funeral Alma told Ruben no, finally, and meant it.

Shaved, in clothes that didn't fit, Cardo left his money on Perla's table, took the dog, and walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the city's edge, with nothing ahead of him and nothing behind worth turning for.

Nadir stood at the counter with Sahar beside him to translate, and the dealer behind the glass did an impression of his accent for the benefit of nobody. He bought the gun anyway. Twice broken into was twice too many.

Later — though Nadir did not know this yet, could not know it, since it hadn't happened — a detective named Reece would kneel by a body in the mud at the edge of a service road and recognize the shoes before he recognized anything else, and understand that the hundred times his mother had asked him to go and look for his brother had finally caught up with him. That was still to come. For now there was only the counter, the mockery, the gun going into a bag.

Two young men, Trey and Kwame, walked up a restaurant pavement arguing about who was watching them, then pulled pistols and took a prosecutor's car off him and his wife at the kerb. The wife, Paula, would stand at the top of her own stairs days later while a locksmith named Mateo fitted new locks, telling her husband, loud enough for Mateo to hear, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys by morning. Mateo went to Nadir's shop after and told him the lock wasn't the problem, the door was. Nadir heard a man inventing himself a second job and threw him out.

Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts for nothing, put Renee on the hood, and searched her with a hand that had no business there while her husband Clay stood three feet off and said nothing. His partner Voss went to their commander the next morning and said he couldn't ride with the man, and got the transfer on the condition he'd blame it on flatulence instead of the truth, and thought that settled something.

Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank, pleading for his father, and got a flat no, and lost his temper at her badge like it had done the refusing.

The shop came apart in the night exactly where Mateo said it would. The insurer read the file and declined, citing the warning Nadir had refused to hear.

Trey and Kwame ran down a small shopkeeper named Pham between parked vans, argued about it for two streets, and left him breathing outside a hospital door — not knowing that his van, found later, would be packed with people paid for in the dark, people Trey would eventually drive to the docks and let go, telling them to run, giving them what was in his pockets.

Clay was pulled from his own car at gunpoint by four officers who'd been told it was stolen, and it was Voss who talked them down. Clay then drove Trey away from a roadblock too fast for either man's comfort and put him out on the verge without a word three miles on.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house all evening with the gun in his coat. When Mateo came out, Nadir raised it and shouted, and Rosie ran off the porch into her father's arms just as it went off. Nothing happened. The girl was unmarked, the father unmarked, and it came out after that Sahar, sent to buy ammunition, had bought the box that does nothing. Nadir called her an angel and meant the child.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain who reached into his pocket, and shot him twice, and burned the car. The hitchhiker was Kwame. This was the body Reece would kneel beside. His mother, on her kitchen floor, told him what she'd told him for years — that she'd asked him to go and look and he never had.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home and lay there until Alba found her, and in the ambulance said the housekeeper she'd insulted for years was the only friend she had.

Boyle, the man who'd assaulted Renee, was the one who crawled into her burning wreck and dragged her out by the belt.

The first snow came. Two cars touched at a junction, and the drivers were shouting before either had looked at the damage.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that crying at other people's funerals-in-advance would put me under for eight hours flat. Support groups for diseases I don't have. I'd sit in the folding chairs and let some woman with real tubes in her arms hold my hand, and something in me would come loose, and I'd sleep like the dead.

Then Ada Vey started coming, smoking through the meditation, faking it worse than I ever could, and the second I could see the lie in her I could see it in myself, and the sleep stopped.

Here is a thing I know now that I didn't know then: at the bottom of a service stairwell, with my own gun in my own mouth, I would understand exactly why a man arrives at that. But that's later. On the flight I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, forty minutes of bad opinions and a good suit, and I kept his card because it seemed important, though I couldn't have said why.

My flat went up while I was away — windows on the pavement, every catalogue thing I owned gone with them — and I didn't call the woman, I called the salesman, and he took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and no explanation.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and I did, and he hit me back, and we lay on the tarmac laughing with blood in our teeth. That became weekly. Weekly became a waiting list. A cellar full of men wanting to be hit by strangers.

He burned my hand with lye once, held it flat on the table and wouldn't let me leave into meditation or breathing or anywhere else. Stay in the minute, he said. I still have the mark. I would still have it, wrapped in gauze, at a window months later watching buildings fall.

Ada overdosed and he brought her back to the house, and for weeks I lay downstairs rigid listening to the two of them through the floors, an arrangement I could not explain being unbearable to me, though it was.

He started rendering stolen surgical fat into soap on the kitchen stove, selling it back at eighty dollars a bar to the stores the women shopped in to afford the surgery in the first place. Money came in. I used my own beaten face on my employer's carpet to buy my absence with a salary.

The house filled with shaved heads who wouldn't speak unless spoken to. He called it Havoc. I couldn't say when it stopped being mine.

He drove into oncoming traffic once, asked the men in back what they wished they'd done, and let the car roll. When I came round in the ditch he was gone and not anywhere.

Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to shut down what I'd made.

City to city after that, I found the same cellar under every bar, the same rules on the same wall, and clerks who looked up and called me Rex Marrow.

In a motel room with flight records fanned over the bedspread it went together at last — one account, one body, one man, awake and asleep, every conversation with the salesman held in an empty room. I called Ada and asked whose bed she'd been in. Mine, she said, obviously. What's wrong with you.

I found the vans wired under the debt-record towers, timed and waiting, and understood the whole shape of it finally, the entire year aimed at one night.

He took me down a stairwell a flight at a time, and at the bottom I understood the gun in his hand was in mine. I put it in my mouth, angled it, and fired through my cheek to kill him.

Ada was brought up by the shaven men, who apologized and left us. We stood at the window holding hands, my face wrapped, and outside the towers went down one after another, in order, exactly on schedule, as if nothing that had happened to me had happened to anyone at all.

Solly Two Coats and his crew went into the diamond house dressed as pilgrims, heads bowed, hands folded, and walked out with the finest stone any of them had ever touched. By the time they reached the street they were laughing.

Overseas, Marv's voice came thin and hard down the line. Bring it straight over, he said. No detours, no cleverness.

In the city, Grigor the Nail was already setting his hooks. He told Solly about a bookmaker who'd take a rich man's bet without asking questions, and in the same breath he told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno about a bookmaker worth robbing. Two errands, one address, and Grigor smiling at both of them.

Meanwhile Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan off the travellers. Sam tried to bully the price down and a bare-knuckle man named Finn put him on the ground with one shot. That left Halloway without a fighter for Coldstone's rigged bout, so he put Finn in instead and swore to the gang boss that Finn would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed in the city that same week, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty case to the bookmaker's, meaning to lay money on the fight himself. Ike, Benno, and a third man called Tulley botched the robbery there — grabbed Solly's arm and his case, panicked, and ran, with Grigor himself chasing them off the street he'd built for them.

In the ring, Finn ignored every instruction and flattened his man in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and turned his fury on Halloway.

Overseas, Marv arrived to find no cousin and no stone, and hired a hunter called Ledge, a man who found the diamond by following the fools who'd touched it.

Grigor took Solly apart to get that case open — cut off his arm for it — and found nothing inside but air.

Ledge, working faster, traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took Ike and Benno and the stone they'd since collected all in one motion.

Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the next fight went wrong. Halloway told Finn to go down in the fourth again — and Coldstone's men answered any doubt by burning Finn's mother alive in her caravan.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno trapped inside. In the gunfire that followed, Ledge died, Grigor died, and Benno died with them, three claims to the diamond ending in the same ditch.

Tulley, the only one of the bunglers left breathing, walked away from the wreck with nothing but a dog — the same dog that had swallowed the stone weeks before, back when the robbery first went wrong.

The rematch came. Finn waited, patient as a debt, until the fourth round exactly — then knocked his man cold anyway, while the travellers he'd grieved with moved through the crowd and cut Coldstone's men down where they stood.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone afterward and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished, wagons and all, as if they'd never come.

Weeks later, a dog was handed in at a pet shop, sick and shivering, and coughed up a diamond onto the counter. It passed, by no plan of anyone's, into the hands of the two promoters who had never stolen anything in their lives, and who now stood holding the one thing that had killed everybody who ever had.

Emlyn came to Wilder's house the same evening, and sat down as if he had merely been asked in for a drink after a long day at the office, and said that he had known for four years. He said Odile had told him on the trip abroad, that first year, in the hotel with the bad plumbing and the view of nothing, and that he had also read the letters — not many, not carefully, but enough. He said he had never thought much of Wilder's letters either, in the way he had never thought much of Wilder's authors, and there was no more heat in it than that. Four years. He let the number sit on the table between them like a bill neither of them had asked to see.

That call had come an hour before, Wilder ringing him in a kind of fright, because Odile had let slip, in the course of telling him her marriage was over, that Emlyn had lately been publishing a writer Wilder represented — a bad writer, one they'd always quietly agreed was bad — and something about the two men's names appearing together on a contract Wilder had never seen undid him more than the marriage news itself.

The marriage news had come the night before that, in a bar, two years after the rooms had closed. She had told him she'd spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband, as though it were the first time, as though four years hadn't already passed under the confession she believed she was only now making. She had said it plainly, almost proudly, the way people announce a decision rather than a memory.

But the rooms had closed long before any of that — the crockery divided on a kitchen table, the lease surrendered without ceremony, because by then the affair had become another set of duties, another household requiring linen counted and afternoons kept, and neither of them had the appetite for it anymore. Before the rooms closed, there had been the dinner at the married couple's house, where the two men talked for two hours about racquets and schoolboy sport and old masters and left Odile no part in it at all, so that she sat at her own table like a guest. Before that, the long lunch, where Emlyn had baited Wilder about contemporary fiction with a viciousness Wilder took for ordinary literary snobbery, never once naming what he knew, though he knew everything by then.

Before that, Odile had gone back to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever of the hotel, of the letter, of her husband's strange calm — and the afternoon had passed exactly as the others had, linen and plates and Wilder none the wiser. Before that, in the hotel abroad, Emlyn had asked at the desk about a letter held for her, addressed in a hand he recognised, and when she confessed he had only said that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife, which was, in its way, the truest thing he ever told her.

Before the hotel there had been the rooms themselves, taken in a quiet district, filled with linen and plates as if ordinary domestic objects could make betrayal into a kind of marriage of its own. Before the rooms, she had told him she was carrying her husband's child, and they had decided, without much discussion, that the rooms would go on exactly as before, as though a child changed the terms of everything except the only thing that mattered.

And before all of it, at the start, a party at Emlyn's own house, drink going round downstairs while Wilder led Odile up to a room and told her how lovely she was, the two men's friendship still whole above them, not yet the shape it would become — comparable, four years later, to two men sitting in a house with a number between them, each having kept a silence for the other's sake, or perhaps only for the pleasure of knowing something the other did not.

Listen: he is unstuck. Not lost, not confused—unstuck, the way a photograph might come loose from an album and fall onto a table of other photographs, so that nobody, including him, can say which one was taken first.

He is shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd. This happens. It has always happened. He knew it would happen the way you know your own name, and when it happens he is not surprised, only briefly inconvenienced by the transition.

He is a boy in a small industrial town, weak and strange, the kind of child other children forget to include in games. His father, believing water teaches courage, throws him into the deep end of a pool. He sinks. At the bottom he discovers something like peace, a place he need not leave. He will remember this feeling for the rest of his life, though "rest of his life" is a phrase that means less to him than it does to you.

He is a chaplain's assistant shipped overseas with no training worth the name. A scout drags him through territory neither of them understands, and when the boy—he is not really a boy now, but he has not stopped being one either—asks to be left to die, the scout beats him for it. They are captured. On the prison train the scout's leg blackens and he dies cursing the man beside him, blaming him with the last air in his lungs.

In the camp, enemy officers eat double rations through a clerical error nobody has bothered to correct, growing plump and glossy while new prisoners arrive gaunt. He is one of the new prisoners. He is sent on to a great city and housed with others in a disused abattoir, a meat locker with a numbered address, and it is there, in the cold beneath the world, that a fellow prisoner tells him: someone will have him killed one day, on the dead scout's account. He does not argue. He has never been good at arguing with certainty.

The city burns in a single night. Fire from above, ash where streets had been. The prisoners climb up from the meat locker into a place that used to have buildings and people and now does not. They are made to dig the dead from cellars until one of the diggers, a young man with an innocent face, dies of the dry heaves, retching at what he uncovers until his body simply stops.

He comes home. He collapses. In the hospital another patient hands him paperbacks by a hack science fiction writer, and something in the cheap, ridiculous prose fits the shape of what happened to him better than any true account could.

He marries the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school. He becomes rich. He is, for years, an ordinary prosperous man with an ordinary prosperous life, and then he survives a plane crash in the mountains while his wife, driving frantically to reach him, dies of exhaust fumes leaking into her car.

He is taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet, alongside a film actress who becomes, in that glass enclosure, both his companion and his exhibit. The aliens explain, patiently, the way one explains something to a child, that every moment that has ever existed exists always, all at once, and that free will is a peculiarity of his own small blue planet's imagination.

He believes them. Listen: he is unstuck. Not lost, not confused—unstuck, the way a photograph might come loose from an album and fall onto a table of other photographs, so that nobody, including him, can say which one was taken first.

He is shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd. This happens. It has always happened. He knew it would happen the way you know your own name, and when it happens he is not surprised, only briefly inconvenienced by the transition.

He is a boy in a small industrial town, weak and strange, the kind of child other children forget to include in games. His father, believing water teaches courage, throws him into the deep end of a pool. He sinks. At the bottom he discovers something like peace, a place he need not leave. He will remember this feeling for the rest of his life, though "rest of his life" is a phrase that means less to him than it does to you.

He is a chaplain's assistant shipped overseas with no training worth the name. A scout drags him through territory neither of them understands, and when the boy—he is not really a boy now, but he has not stopped being one either—asks to be left to die, the scout beats him for it. They are captured. On the prison train the scout's leg blackens and he dies cursing the man beside him, blaming him with the last air in his lungs.

In the camp, enemy officers eat double rations through a clerical error nobody has bothered to correct, growing plump and glossy while new prisoners arrive gaunt. He is one of the new prisoners. He is sent on to a great city and housed with others in a disused abattoir, a meat locker with a numbered address, and it is there, in the cold beneath the world, that a fellow prisoner tells him: someone will have him killed one day, on the dead scout's account. He does not argue. He has never been good at arguing with certainty.

The city burns in a single night. Fire from above, ash where streets had been. The prisoners climb up from the meat locker into a place that used to have buildings and people and now does not. They are made to dig the dead from cellars until one of the diggers, a young man with an innocent face, dies of the dry heaves, retching at what he uncovers until his body simply stops.

He comes home. He collapses. In the hospital another patient hands him paperbacks by a hack science fiction writer, and something in the cheap, ridiculous prose fits the shape of what happened to him better than any true account could.

He marries the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school. He becomes rich. He is, for years, an ordinary prosperous man with an ordinary prosperous life, and then he survives a plane crash in the mountains while his wife, driving frantically to reach him, dies of exhaust fumes leaking into her car.

He is taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet, alongside a film actress who becomes, in that glass enclosure, both his companion and his exhibit. The aliens explain, patiently, the way one explains something to a child, that every moment that has ever existed exists always, all at once, and that free will is a peculiarity of his own small blue planet's imagination.

He believes them.
